utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone on this last day in court before the recess. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. May I first inquire of the parties whether additional talks yesterday have resulted in anything the Chamber should know?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, they have. We have agreed upon the date of the 10th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is for the -- to object to the admission of pending exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 10th of August. And may I then take it that any responses within two days from the 10th of August?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would be perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I also take it that this agreement includes acceptance of what the Chamber said earlier, that we are not confronted at a later stage from this point, at least, that further time would be needed to prepare for the final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. That's my understanding, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not on this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I specifically said on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to confirm that I registered that, Your Honour. May ask then, inquire, it's a small point that's arisen. I'd like clarity just between Mr. Harmon and myself, we were not sure between ourselves whether the current date ordered for filing of the final briefs was now Thursday the 17th or Friday the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I would be grateful, Your Honour, just to -- for us to be informed what's in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meanwhile can inform the parties that the dates, the 29th and the 30th and the 31st of August, where the Chamber had difficulties finding a courtroom, that finally this has been settled so that these dates are now firm. The Chamber did not receive any other housekeeping matters to be discussed at this moment. And I checked until five minutes ago, so unless I hear otherwise, I take it that there will be no further housekeeping matters to be raised. I have, however, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there is just the issue of the introduction of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Those two remaining exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will deliver a decision on some exhibits right now. But I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would rather deal with those after the break but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, further argument on exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's not so much as argument, Your Honour. There are two that the Defence wish to introduce, which is the bridge video in part, which has been agreed in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And also there is the Islamic declaration. There is some discussion rather than dispute at the bar as to whether all 77 pages that have been translated by the CLSS should be admitted or only portions. In short, Your Honour, the Defence are simply seeking to put in a few selected portions. But frankly, if my learned friends say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, Mr. Josse. You said that was the Islamic declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So in short the Defence simply are seeking to put in a few selected portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But if the Prosecution would rather that the whole document was admitted in the event the Defence is seeking admission of part, then I don't suppose we are in a position to oppose that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps better addressed after the break. It's just that we are quite anxious to know what we need to provide the Court with at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Harmon, Mr. Tieger, any clear position yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the issue would merit some further discussions with counsel and then we -- we are anxious at this point to review the selections that have been made by the Defence and assess those selections in relation to the complete document. We have not arrived at a decision yet on whether we agree that only select the portions should be put in or the whole document. So we would ask that a decision, that further discussions take place, and that we -- Your Honours defer a decision on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that it would still be an option that the Prosecution instead of insisting on the whole of the document being admitted select their portions, which they find of importance, and then this would be a way of limiting the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That would be an option to that would be acceptable to us then if we select portions we would share them with our colleagues from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've got a practical suggestion, perhaps I can make it at the break to my learned friend and we can return to the subject before the court rises at the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm pleased that it was to some extent useful to briefly discuss it at this moment. About the -- which negotiations the video --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can tell you where we are, Your Honour, we have exchanged translations. The Defence has prepared translations of portions of that video. This morning I had my language assistant assess that translation and whether it was complete or accurate, and I then received a copy of a -- some addition that is were made to that that had been submitted to me by the Defence, that translation, and I e-mailed it to the Defence. Again, I haven't heard from the Defence yet whether those amendments are accepted or not but after the break I'm sure we can resolve that issue as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to make the same practical suggestion in relation to that and if that's acceptable, we will pledges to the Chamber later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sounds very reasonable. Then I'll read a decision on the request by the Defence for additional time and evidence. And meanwhile, I'll ask Mr. Usher to already keep the witness standby. The Chamber would like to deliver a decision on various requests by the Defence for additional time and evidence and for excluding the evidence related to Chamber Witness Mrs. Plavsic. On the 30th of June 2006, the Defence filed a motion for time to call further Defence witnesses, requesting an additional 57 and a half additional hours in order to call witnesses out of a list of 18 named individuals. The Prosecution responded on the 10th of July 2006, and the Defence replied on the 11th of July. The motion is denied and written reasons will follow in due course. On the 30th of June, 2006, the Defence also filed a motion pursuant to Rule 85 requesting additional time to provide information relevant to sentence, should the accused be found guilty. In particular, the Defence seeks two full days to call viva voce evidence and present information as well as the possibility to submit, and I quote, "Written testimonials." The motion is denied in so far as it relates to viva voce evidence. With respect to written documentation, the Chamber is in no position to make a determination until the proposed material is identified. The Chamber therefore allows the Defence, if it so wishes to provide this material by the 31st much July 2006 and the Prosecution to respond if it so wishes by the 4th of August. If the dates are such that the parties could agree or would agree on a similar date as for the other material, then the Chamber will consider such a joint suggestion by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt save for the fact that the practical problems that we've alluded two on these two occasions earlier this week, apply so far as this is concerned, and it's essential, frankly, from our point of view for that order to be remotely effective or for there to be some sort of extension. I see my learned friend is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In light of those problems of which we are aware and we have discussed before I'm confident we can reach an agreement similar to the one outlined in the court earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that especially in that respect, that the problems that would arise from this late filing would not create major problems for final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as the Court noted we haven't seen the material but we can't -- we don't anticipate such problems, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I note that there are comments in the Prosecution's response to our motion, and frankly, we appreciate what is said, appreciate what my learned friend has just said, and I can't imagine there will be any problems either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I'll continue with delivering the decision. Finally, on the 11th of July, 2006, the Defence filed a motion to exclude all evidence related to the Chamber witness, Biljana Plavsic, and for prospective witness, Branko Djeric, not to be called as a witness. The Chamber dismissed the part of the motion related to Mr. Djeric on the same day. Due to the circumstances and the timing of the motion, the Chamber will now issue an oral decision with respect to the testimony of Mrs. Plavsic without having heard from the Prosecution. That part of the motion is also denied. Reasons will follow in writing. With respect to the exhibits related to the testimony of Mrs. Plavsic, the Chamber has given the parties until - and I draw the attention of the interpreters to the fact that the dates are not as written down - has given the parties until the 10th of August 2006, and that is on today's transcript, to object to the admission of all pending exhibits and until the 12th of August to respond to any objections from the opposing party. This deadline applies to exhibits related to all Chamber witnesses including Mrs. Plavsic. There concludes the Chamber's decision on various requests, motions by the Defence. And the Chamber would now like to briefly address the parties regarding exhibits -- Exhibit D254 which is a video clip with an interview of General MacKenzie played in court on the 19th of June 2006. The Chamber has been informed by the Defence that the parties have agreed that court transcript of the 19th of June will suffice for their purposes in lieu of an official English transcript from CLSS. The Chamber accepts this practical solution as well and does not insist on an additional English transcript. The Chamber was informed that meanwhile the video clip has been provided to the registrar. Lastly, regarding the documents and CDs which were provided to the registrar by Mr. Krajisnik during his testimony, and here I'm referring to those items which were not assigned any exhibit number, and not tendered into evidence by either of the parties, the registrar is hereby instructed to return these items to Mr. Krajisnik at the first convenient opportunity. This concludes the delivery of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My client might need a form for those in order for him to be readmitted to the Detention Unit. I'm sure Mr. Haider will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The practicalities, I also assume they will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise one point in connection with the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I appreciate that the Court throughout the discussion of this issue has remained concerned about issues related to the closing briefs and closing arguments and of course my comments have to be made in light of the Court's anticipatory awareness of that throughout but if I understand it correctly, now, the Court will be essentially seized of the -- of any issues arising from that on the 12th. The Court is aware of the deadline dates for the final brief, and I think there was an anticipation or expectation that the Court would be in a position to respond to any such issues forthwith so that the parties would at least have an opportunity to adjust, if necessary, in one way or another, to any aspects that might be affected in connection with the final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will be here on these dates and will be in a position to respond on shortest notice and the parties may be aware that the Chamber sometimes is developing some speed in that respect. Finally, final briefs are expected by the 18th of August. 18th of August. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Djeric into the courtroom? THE USHER: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- has the time further been discussed between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour, and in that connection I want to express my appreciation to Mr. Stewart. The situation is this: I will make every effort to conclude within the time also graciously allotted by the Trial Chamber, that is the 15 minutes. Mr. Stewart has indicated, however, that if another 15 minutes was needed that it wouldn't impact in any way -- any adverse way on his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Djeric, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is that you'll speak the truth, and I emphasise the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On Thursday, the 13th of July, that is yesterday, you were asked some questions by His Honour Judge Orie concerning reports from Mr. Stanisic. That began at the bottom of page 15 of the transcript and continued on roughly through page 16 and 17. You indicated -- the Judge asked you at one point did you ever receive written reports on the security of people and property. You said sometimes I did, sometimes it took a while, sometimes they would be detailed, sometimes they would be quite brief. And His Honour asked you about the kind of information in those reports -- there is nothing to react to yet until I finish, please. The Judge asked you approximately what kind of information was in those reports, you said I really cannot -- I cannot remember, it was a long time ago. There were lots of strictly confidential, all these abbreviations were used so I cannot remember. There were some further discussion about that. In that connection, Mr. Djeric, I wanted to show you two items. The first is found at tab 58 of the binders. That bundle may not have been distributed yet. And the second should be distributed now. We can give those both numbers and the witness can have them both before him, in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they already in evidence, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me check, Your Honour, I believe they both need numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For tab 58, yes. And, Mr. Registrar, may I take it that P1291 would be the other document, bulletin of daily incidents number 73, strictly confidential, 24th of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Djeric, P1290 and P1291 are two daily reports or bulletins from the MUP, 1290 is from April 1992, the 22nd and 23rd. P1291 is from July 1992, the 24th of July to be specific, and I'd like you to take a quick look at those, looking first at P1290, the April report. That reflects information concerning a number of municipalities, including Banja Luka, Sanski Most, Trebinje, Gacko, Bijeljina, and Zvornik. And P1291, the July report, similarly contains information regarding a number of municipalities, including quite recent activities as we see from the second paragraph about 0400 and 0600 hours, this area, et cetera, reference to the security -- the complex security situation in Rajlovac and Vogosca, the complex security situation at the bottom of the paragraph on page 2 and the page -- on page 6471 of your version, in Sekovici, and the last paragraph of that section before the discussion about Trebinje, reflects actions taken in Pale, Sokolac, Han Pijesak, and Rogatica, to cleanse the remaining Muslim extremists, weapons being confiscated. There are -- there is information later in the report, as you can see, on other areas including Srebrenica, Kotor Varos, Banja Luka, et cetera. Mr. Djeric, are these -- do these -- are these the kinds of reports that you were referring to in responding to the questions by His Honour yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't remember such documents. Because these are documents that have to do with the military part, the part that has to do with weapons, and I have to tell you that the Ministry of the Interior did not have any such obligation vis-a-vis the government. That part of the police and that work was under the president. That is to say the military and the use of police in wartime was under the president. You see that this is not addressed to the government. It's simply not sent to the government at all. This is the first time I see this type of report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You told His Honour -- I mean, the questioning yesterday was in connection with reports on matters such as the security of people and property. Then you went on to the explanation about the frequency of the reports and the detail of those reports. What information did you receive sometimes in detail, sometimes not, about the security of people and property that differed from the kind of information contained here in P1290 and 1291?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, these were reports that were related to, well, the situation in the MUP, the needs of the MUP, I mean things like that. Supplies, equipment and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to -- that may be -- all right. Doesn't quite answer my question. My question was, you indicated yesterday that you received reports, sometimes in detail, sometimes brief, with lots of strictly confidential material about the security of people and property. How did the information you received about the security of people differ from the kinds of information contained here which seems to be about that, at least in part?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I cannot recall the details now. Do you understand what I'm saying? But I know that information was sought, for instance, about the situation in, I mean, well, the reception centres. Well, that's what I meant. I mean -- and sort of things like that. Well, I mean, at any rate, I'm saying to you that the information that came to the government was of a different nature. There information, as presented here, perhaps went to the president. I don't know. I mean -- or it was used within the MUP but I did not encounter this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You've made repeated references to the -- during the course of your testimony to the information sought about the reception centres. I recall, for example, that on repeated occasions on the first day of your testimony, which I believe was the 12th, in discussing the journalists' reports about the camps, you referred to the -- your request for reports about the centres. That was at page 58. Discussed it again on page 60. You set up a commission to receive better information about the camps. And again on I think page 73, and 76, you seem to allude to those reports. Since I have very little time, let me discuss that with you briefly now. The Trial Chamber's materials which it didn't -- earlier prepared materials, I believe, contained D246, which is a letter of August 7th, 1992, that refers to a copy of reports on the situation in Manjaca and Bileca prisons. It's a letter to you from Dr. Karadzic dated the 7th of August which, of course, is the same date as the press release that we looked at yesterday and that the Court examined with you the day before that. If I -- at this point, I'd like to present you with that letter plus the report it refers to. And those will need -- the D246 obviously doesn't need a number, Your Honour, but the report will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the report --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will be P1292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a report numbered 01456-92 dated the 7th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, the situation we have -- for the record, the number the Court just resided appears on the letter from Dr. Karadzic which is P246 and I think this should -- might as well be exhibited in its entirety - that is the letter and the report that is attached - but just so the record is clear, this initial letter, this one-page letter on the top, is also D246.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So now attached to this letter, and perhaps we have that letter in again under the new number, P1292. We find behind it a letter in which the International Committee of the Red Cross sends a -- sends its observations concerning the visit to Manjaca, to the president of the Serbian Democratic Party. Copies sent to Mr. Koljevic, Ms. Plavsic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you recall receiving the letter from Dr. Karadzic and the report by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see -- all right. Did you ever hear about the substance of the findings of the ICRC from Dr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, or Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You can see that everybody dealt with different matters there. You see? You see President Karadzic, he's dealing with these issues. These overall issues. And usually I mean -- well, he used Kalinic for that and the Minister of the Interior, if security questions related to camps are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in this particular case, it seems that Dr. Karadzic at least prepared a letter to you and sent you this report but let's look quickly at the substance of the report and let me ask you this. Do you recall hearing from any source, and in particular any member of the Bosnian Serb leadership, that the ICRC had visited Manjaca camp in mid-July 1992, that is the 14th through the 16th, and that during the course of that visit, every one of the delegates who visited observed frequent and widespread traces of recent and often severe beatings of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing from any source, including the ones I mentioned, that many detainees showed marked weight loss, signs of anaemia with severity often corresponding to the length of detention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you knew nothing according to you about the many prisoners who were suffering from chronic physical or mental illnesses in Manjaca camp and Bileca camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't know. I'm talking in the context of these letters, you know. I mean, in the context of these letters. I mean, the world press is a different thing. I told you about that already. I told you the other day. As for these questions, you can see here, it was President Karadzic that dealt with them. Then Kalinic dealt with this in some domains the minister the interior, too, so this was sent to them, you see?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I recited some of your references to the commission reports, that is the government commission reports. Were those commissions sent to the camps to determine whether allegations made by representatives of the international community, and representatives of the international media, were true and, if so, to remedy those conditions and to hold accountable those persons responsible? Is that what those commissions were about or were they for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of those commissions was to tour the camps to improve the situation, then further on, if necessary, to disband some and so on. And I mean, well, a group would usually be formed from people from the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And among the allegations of the international community and international media was that prisoners and detainees were mistreated and that civilians were held in those facilities. Was there any effort according to you by the government or any other body of the Bosnian Serb authorities, to determine whether those allegations were true and to hold accountable those persons responsible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I mean, these groups were set up to tour and to provide the government with information and within that context, we adopted some conclusions; that is, to improve the situation, then that certain camps be disbanded, all in keeping with the findings of those working groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This Court has had an opportunity to review the reports prepared by the government commissions. You can have a chance to look at those now if you wish. Those include the report by Vojin Lale and Mirko Erkic [phoen] on August 17th, I think, the report by Mr. Avlijas on August 22nd and the subsequent report on October 22nd, again, if I recall correctly, by Mr. Avlijas. Those commission reports do not appear to reflect any effort whatsoever to investigate the issue of responsibility for maltreatment, responsibility for detention of civilians. Are you aware of any other reports, and can you tell the Court what those are, that addressed those issues?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when it came to these issues, I was not informed in any other way but through the working groups, through the feedback, but I always put pressure on the ministries, the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice, I repeat, to work in the field on all of the issues pertaining to their purview and to act in the way that the -- a state with the rule of law should function, and amongst other things, this was a constant problem in the functioning of the government. But you see from these reports, i.e., from the work of these groups, that we did work, that we did send teams all the time. I mean, that we did have information about all that. In other words, we were not passive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no doubt you had information, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I've used my time, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One additional question, Mr. Djeric, in this respect. You say look at these documents, you see it was Karadzic and it was the others I think it was Kalinic and the others, they were addressed, they dealt with the matter. But of course, one would be inclined to say, "Look at the documents. You were addressed in a letter by Mr. Karadzic." Do you see the problem we might have, that if you rely upon what is written down, that how could we do that if you say, well, what's written down to the extent that others were dealing with the matter, just look at the paper, and as far as the papers or this letter indicates that copies of the reports of the ICRC are sent to you, you say, well, don't know about it. Reports, including malnutrition, detention of insane people but also civilian detainees of which the ICRC says, "Release them."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, I don't see -- actually I do see that the Presidency did write to Mr. Samaruga, and then it says here "the government," and it says we expect the government to engage the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior and undertake all the necessary measures. And so on and so forth. Pursuant to all that, the groups were set up eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- let me simply stop you there for a second. I see a letter from the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with a signature and a stamp under it which suggests that this letter was signed by Radovan Karadzic and it's addressed to the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Branko Djeric, Prime Minister, first line being, "Dear Mr. Prime Minister. I hereby deliver to you copies of the reports of the situation in Manjaca and Bileca prisons that I just received." And then he tells that he has sent a letter to Mr. Samaruga and Mr. Mladic. So it seems that this report at least that is what this letter says, is directly sent to you, not to the government in general, but to the Prime Minister, Mr. Branko Djeric. The report says that civilian detainees are recommended by the ICRC to be released. So therefore, you say that you -- committees were supposed to tour the camps and you draw our attention to the fact, who was dealing with the matter. But these papers, this letter, suggests that you were supposed to deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I mean, the government. The government set up the working groups consisting of the ministries of justice and the Interior so it was the government in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that caused by the receipt of this letter and this report by Mr. Karadzic, the report by the ICRC and the letter sent to you by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the context -- I mean, I don't remember the details of this. I said there were the writings of the world press and, simply put, it is possible that the ministers, since they were in contact with the President Karadzic also were informed about all this. In other words, I don't remember the details thereof but I remember that we acted urgently in order to deal with those issues, and exactly certain ministers were required to tour, to see, to look at the situation, and to see what they could do to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there ever -- was it ever ordered that civilian detainees should be released immediately? Which is a clear recommendation of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. I don't know that. This was not within my purview. I did not have the means to order anything, to issue any orders. In other words, I could not issue any orders to either the military or to the police or to any of those who held that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart is it you or is it Mr. Josse who is going to examine the witness? Mr. Josse comes in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Fortunately it's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: For today's hearing, anyway, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- hold my hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, good afternoon. Mr. Djeric you were a member of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina back in early 1991 and onwards, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who nominated you or put you forward or that position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position as a member of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly the one I was asking about, yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nominated by my party. I was on the list of the party that was represented by Karadzic and it was that party that nominated me as a member of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But who as an individual, if you can remember, first approached you with a view to your possibly becoming a member of that government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember. I don't know who it was who was in charge of the personnel policy. I don't even think that that was organised in that way. It was rather diffuse. Everybody could nominate any candidates before the president of the party and then he will be the one who selected and proposed. I remember that he invited me, I went to visit him, and thereafter followed the final nomination. Who was it who spoke to him about me as a possible candidate, I really can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your colleagues in that government included, didn't they, as Serb members, Mr. Simovic. Tell me if you remember this. Mr. Simovic? Agreed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Ranko Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Momcilo Pejic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Miljivojen Nadezdin [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. David Balaban?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anybody else that you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you mention Bozo Rantic [phoen] at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I hadn't. So you remember him, do you, as having a government post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about who first approached any of those gentlemen to become members of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it, if you do know, was it the rather -- were they part of the rather diffuse process that you mentioned a few minutes ago, where everybody could nominate anybody and then the president of the party would select and propose?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that's how things were. Different authorities proposed to the president of the party, because everybody had some interest in proposing people, and I really don't know how all this was organised, how it all went.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you were then subsequently a member of the Bosnian Serb council of ministers, as it's called, from December 1991 onwards, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you remember how you became a member of that council?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply pursuant to the decisions of the Assembly of the Serbian People, I -- pursuant to the decision of the Assembly of the Serb People of Republika Srpska, all the ministers that constituted the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina were at the same time members of the ministerial council of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was as simple as that, was it, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how it was, because the Serbian Republic was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, these ministers were at the same time members of the ministerial council and members of the government and they attended the sessions of the -- both bodies. It was vice-president Simovic, the vice Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina who chaired the meetings of the ministerial council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were the Minister of Development, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the same thing I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How active, if indeed it was active, was the council of ministers from December 1991 through to March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was active. I can't speak about that, but they had to report to somebody. I don't know who to. I can only say that there was a certain activity, that this body was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you an active participant?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, my position was without a portfolio so that I -- as to the extent needed I was present. My sector was not important because not much was said about development at the time, we were facing a crisis. The most important sectors was the interior, finances and some economic sectors where there was money, like, for example, transport, agriculture, forestry and so on. A ministry without portfolio -- actually this was not a ministry as such; there was just a minister. In other words, I was by myself in that ministry, with a secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we just be clear, because it's certainly been suggested in the course of the Prosecution case --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I was looking at Mr. Treanor's report --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That you were the minister of development. Were you technically the minister of development or were you technically a minister without portfolio?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, I was a minister without a portfolio. That was the official title, a minister without a portfolio, but I was interested in the issues of development. And let me also tell you that before the war, I was the head of a team that worked on the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was a government programme, and this programme was well received by all the factors, by all the three sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was in other words my engagement. That's where my engagement was. The government programme of development strategy which was a well-received programme at the moment when it was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, when that council of ministers was replaced by the Bosnian Serb government and we have seen that, you became the president or Prime Minister, Mr. Pejic was the vice-president at first. Were you content with Mr. Pejic as your vice-president or Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truth be told, he was an invalid. I don't know whether he became vice-Prime Minister immediately. I can't remember. I believe it was somewhat later. In other words he had a severe handicap and a severe disability, and he went to Belgrade very soon after that and he was there in Belgrade in the office of the government. In other words, he had a disability. He was disabled. And, of course, with him, I was not very happy with him. But the situation was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, can we be clear? First of all, Mr. Pejic had been the Minister of Finance in the Bosnia and Herzegovina government, hadn't he, from January 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the Finance Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, apart from any difficulties such as you've just mentioned which might have affected his practical ability to do the work, were you otherwise content with Mr. Pejic as your deputy in the newly formed government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wasn't in practical terms -- you understand, he was in Belgrade and the Minister of Finance was Petra Markovic and she worked in the inner government. In other words, I was not especially satisfied because this person was ill, he had a disability, he was an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've told us that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But simply put --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You told us about that, Mr. Djeric. You were content with Mrs. Markovic, were you, then, as the Minister of Finance?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she -- she was healthy and she did her job. She was always present.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was it then Mr. Pejic's health difficulties that you've referred to which led to him being quite quickly replaced on the 8th of June, it appears, by Mr. Trbojevic as the vice-president or Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was not Trbojevic actually. It was not Trbojevic who was Deputy Prime Minister. Let me put it simply. In practical terms, the Prime Minister was helped with Deputy Prime Ministers in charges of certain sectors. For example, Trbojevic could stand in for the Prime Minister if the issues at stake were in the interior. I was absent. But if the issues were of an economic nature then he couldn't do it. Trbojevic was in the inner government and he might have used that and that is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djeric, I'll invite to you consider, is that right? It appears that from evidence that has been received in this case, that Mr. Trbojevic was quite clearly and formally appointed the vice-president of the government by a decision of the 8th of June. Does that ring a bell, now I've put it that way? Do you think that might be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, he was appointed the vice-president, but I don't remember anybody ever mentioning a deputy. Birus [phoen] also was vice-president. There were two vice-presidents, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- it is quite correct and I've just -- you needn't I think look at the document, Mr. Djeric, and probably nobody else has to immediately, but 21st government meeting of Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina held on the 5th of June, you chaired the meeting as president of the government, and it said, also present, vice-presidents of the government, Milan Trbojevic -- excuse me one moment, Your Honour. There may be a -- there may be a point on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll come back to that, Your Honour. It's possible there a simple misprint so rather than waste time on that I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you presumably were in the light of what you have said, you were content and in no unkind way, content that Mr. Pejic left the government, were you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not understand you properly, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was not -- as far as you were concerned, it was not a negative -- well first of all, Mr. Pejic did leave the government, didn't he? Quite soon after it was formed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, I don't remember whether he left. I don't think he left. He was still on the list as vice-president of the government, but his purview pertained to the job of the head of office of the government in Belgrade. So nobody took that away from him, as far as I can remember. He just wasn't the Finance Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, your colleague, Mr. Nadazdin, who was in the Bosnian Serb government from May 1992 onwards, you had no problems with him, did you, as one of those ministers who had been in the Bosnia and Herzegovina government and continued into your government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just can't remember Nadazdin at this point somehow because he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Minister of Agriculture forestry and water works, does that trigger any memory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that, and he joined somewhat later and then he reported to the headquarters of the government and I don't know how long he stayed. This is what I'm saying. I don't know how long he stayed in the position as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Dr. Aleksa Milojevic, do you remember what post he had?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the government, our government. He was the minister that we called the minister without portfolio, minister for development. This is what he dealt in. He dealt in the theoretical issues of privatisation and he also belonged to the government but just like Pejic he also stayed in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about Dr. Kalinic, do you remember Dr. Kalinic as being a member of your government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He was also a member of the government. He was a -- the minister for health, social policies, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he effective?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, he was there. Well, he worked but he was also quite close to the president and to the Presidency. He was up there all the time. He liked being there. But, I mean, he was in the ministry too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You didn't have any special problems with Dr. Kalinic, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, well, special ones? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about Mr. Professor Zukovic, what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was minister of education, that is to say minister for schools and education. I mean, well, he dealt with education issues and questions from that portfolio generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was he effective?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he displayed a certain industriousness in terms of establishing laws or rather adopting laws, organising schools, well, textbooks, and so on and so forth. He worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Lajic, Nedeljko Lajic, do you remember his post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was minister for transportation and communication. And he was always in the centre of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was he effective, then?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, under the given circumstances, as they were, I mean, in view of all sorts of problems, and a breakdown in communications, in energy pipelines, and so on and so forth, under those circumstances, well, he did, well, he did, well, as I said, I mean, he worked and he did quite a bit under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic, of course, was carrying through the same basic job, wasn't he, as Minister of Information that he had had since January 1991 in the Bosnia-Herzegovina government, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, well, yes. His field was information. He was a journalist otherwise. That was right up his alley. Yes. Well, he was sort of exposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He was the obvious person to take this post in the newly formed Bosnian Serb government, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, quite simply, he was a man who was trusted by the party president. He was a party man. I think he was a member of these uppermost organs of the party. He was always in direct contact with the party leadership and the Presidency. Well, that is to say that in a way he was more in the Presidency than he was in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But when he became a member of the government, you had no reason not to trust him, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I could not not trust him. Do you realise I was simply not in that position. I had people made available to me. I mean, quite simply, that's the way it was out there at that time. At that time. I mean, it's different when you have well-established states based on the rule of law; when it's different, when you have a Prime Minister designate who knows about people, who is aware of their CVs and so on. He has various possibilities. I had no such possibilities. I got people who had been in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, well, yes, in addition to the government, I mean people who had been nominated by the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, when you accepted the position as president or Prime Minister of the government of the Bosnian Serb republic, we can take it, can we, that whatever misgivings you might have had here and there, you were broadly satisfied with the group of people that you were being given as your ministers. Would you -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, that issue was not even being raised. It was never opened. A government was established out of ministers who had been members of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I mean, well, in that situation, I couldn't do a thing. I could only later, when I saw that some ministries were not functioning, I could simply, well, leave. I mean, at that time. But at this point in time, well, it was about people who were already members of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djeric, I'm going to suggest to you one thing you could have done because in your last answer you said you could simply, well, leave. At the very beginning, do you agree, if you had not been broadly satisfied with the group of people that you were being asked to lead as the Prime Minister, you could and would and should have simply said, "No, I won't be Prime Minister." Isn't that -- isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but I didn't know people. You see? Do you understand what I'm saying? There were people there who I didn't know. Well, I mean, later, when I got to know some of these ministers, I would not have worked with these people at any cost. Another thing you have to know: A person needs years and years to get to know someone. And I knew these people only for a very short period of time, very short. Some of them I practically did not know at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's be very clear then. Who are the people you would not have worked with at any cost if you had known what you came to know? Let's have names, please, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, with Mandic, Stanisic. I wouldn't work with the two of them. Well, I wouldn't work with Trbojevic either, and I mean, well, the -- the minister for the military, I mean, well, quite simply, he got into a clash with the military. He was on the sidelines all the time. I wouldn't work with people like that either. I mean, how should we put this? If they cannot get to the right places, you can't work with people like that either. Then, with these sick people either, Pejic objectively speaking, wouldn't do. Now I'd really have to look at this individually from one person to another. I'm telling you -- well, I wouldn't work with those people who very soon set out to Belgrade with their wives and were not at the seat of the government at all. This government worked only with part of the ministers that were at the seat of the government. I mean, say, four or five of them. The others were not there. And always, well, they were covered up for by the top political leadership. They are in Belgrade, they have this kind of work, that kind of work and so on and so forth. That was the case with Buha. That was the case with Milojevic. Well, yeah. Pejic and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you think, on reflection, Mr. Djeric, that frankly, at this time, in these very difficult circumstances, this government in the Bosnian Serb republic just needed a tougher person at the head than you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, well, I mean, well, as far as I'm concerned, well, it wasn't up to me. I mean, well, it's not me. It's not the Prime Minister. That's not the issue. The issue is -- I mean, well, the issue is the question of the Presidency, because had the government not been hindered from there and had it not been sidelined from there it would have been a completely different government. That has nothing to do with anything. Perhaps the resoluteness of the Prime Minister in persevering along the lines of a state based on the rule of law was the reason for well, I mean -- well, for these problems that the government encountered. I keep telling you the government was sidelined. You know, people know where power lies. People know when they go towards an office, they know whether there is power in that office. Then they believe in those people who are in that office. You know, I as Prime Minister did not attend meetings with international factors, with UNPROFOR, with the military representatives coming from abroad. Then these people, well, I mean, politicians and so on. I did not take part in the peace negotiations. You can establish all of that. I was thrown out, thrown out, precisely because of my toughness and stamina. How else can you interpret this? How can you think that I was fighting the president of the republic? How can there be that kind of concept if I'm not tough? How should I put this? If I'm not someone who is capable of leading a government. This has to do with certain people, certain ministers, who had support from the president of the party, from the party itself. I mean, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying, Mr. Djeric, you're -- let's get clear. Your assessment of yourself and this time that you were in government and the circumstances in which you ceased to be Prime Minister, are that you were thrown out because you were too tough? That's your assessment, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying too tough. I mean, I, well, I was asking for a delineation of powers. One should know what the executive, what the judiciary and what the legislative branches of government are. How should I put this? Karadzic thought this -- this was a presidential system. That he was the government, that he was ruling. And that ministers should orient themselves towards him. That's where they were -- well, I told you about that yesterday. The government was 12 kilometres away from the Presidency. Well, in the Presidency there was Karadzic, then the president of the assembly and two members of the Presidency of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, Plavsic and Koljevic. So they were - how should I put it? - this nucleus. The government and the Prime Minister were 12 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, your successor, your immediate successor as Prime Minister, was Mr. Vladimir Lukic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how he came to be -- I'm not talking about the formal voting. We can leave that to one side. Do you know how he came to be your immediate successor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know very much. I heard that at the proposal of Koljevic, he was nominated, appointed. Now, is that correct, is that not correct? I don't know. Was it because he was from a different region, not the one where the seat of the government was, I don't know. I really don't know the details. Well, I'm saying what I heard, that Koljevic practically promoted him and spoke for him to Karadzic and that is how he was nominated. Now, I don't know whether that's the way it actually was or whether it was not that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock and I've finished that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart just for our own information, we have taken now approximately one hour and a half, we usually have a break, half an hour, 25 minutes, half an hour, then have another session of approximately one hour and a half and then have a bit of a shorter session at the end. If you would say, if I would continue for another ten minutes, for example, and then have perhaps also a second session which is slightly longer than one hour and a half, if you would say then we would finish, because you know the last session will be shorter anyhow because we have to finish at 6.30, then we could see whether we could do with one break and two slightly extended sessions. If you say no, that's not possible, then of course we'll have a break now. If you consider this to be a possibility, I would like to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'd put right out of my mind, Your Honour, that it does make a practical difference on our side of the court, whether we break before 4.00 or not but your leaving aside that small practical matter. The fact is, Your Honour, I would expect to finish comfortably and with any questions that Your Honour is permitted to Mr. Krajisnik would expect to finish comfortably before the next break anyway if we just proceed in the normal course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we just proceed now according to the normal course, Your Honour, I'm confident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break now, and we'll have a break for half an hour. We will resume at 20 minutes past four past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'm going to hand you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour we photocopied this for convenience of all concerned. It's P65 binder 12, tab 160. There is an English and a B/C/S version clipped together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, while you're obviously very sensitive looking at your the copy in your own language at the back, could you just take a minute to familiarise yourself with that. Let us know, please, whether you've had that chance.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, is that first of all is that document at all familiar to you, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's, as you can see, an order on applying the international laws of war on the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, showing it's been signed by Dr. Karadzic 13th of June 1992. Can -- is it that you just don't remember about such a document or are you saying that you never knew anything about any such document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest with you, it wasn't sent to me. I believe that he did that but I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You have a --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it may have gone to the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior but not to the government, and on this occasion, I take the opportunity to remind you of the -- of the overall situation, you know. Anybody could take something from the president or the Presidency and take that directly to their own ministry, bypassing the Prime Minister in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we just be clear, Mr. Djeric? Is it that you say of this period 14 years ago that you are completely confident when you look at a document like this that it was never sent to you or is it that you just don't remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I mean, I don't remember. And by the nature of things, these things did not have anything whatsoever to do with me and they could have something to do with the war -- Ministry of the Interior, in other words the police, and the military, and this may -- might have gone directly to either of the two ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is nothing in this document which would have caused you any concern if you had known about it, is there, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you, sir. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you would have -- if you had specifically seen this document, you would have approved of it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I am not qualified to approve any of these documents. It was up to the certain ministries, and subjects that those things applied to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, would you please carefully listen to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because the question was reading the content of it, whether you are happy with it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to rephrase in a similar way. Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So looking at the content, do you say, well, this is fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would have been the right thing, wouldn't it, Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I can talk only about the spirit of the document. In other words, my position is that one has to comply the rules of the international law, in the spirit of the document, that is, and as for certain details, I can't, about that I can't say anything about that. This applies to the military personnel and the police officers. As for the spirit of the document, absolutely, strict compliance with the international law, if I understood you correctly, that is. And that means whoever violates the rules of the international law, those people have to be taken to task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to a different topic, Mr. Djeric. Did you sometime in -- and I'm going to suggest to you it was July 1992 -- receive any report relating to the treatment of Mr. Ostojic by a group known as the yellow wasps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were rumours that he was stopped somewhere on the Drina, and that allegedly he was forced to -- actually he was ill treated. This is what I heard. He was also a bit extremist himself. It resounded quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can clear up, please, what you're saying there. When you said he was also a bit extremist, himself, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in many things, he was extreme. Firstly, in party terms, his only concern was the party and so on and so forth. How shall I put it? He was rather exclusive and he was always in conflict with journalists and that are the reason for which I would never want to see him in the government. He was of extreme views with regard to many of the things that the government fought for. He was always against many things, and he was the first among those who were against me when I resigned. A while ago you asked me about me being firm. In your view, would I have been firm if I had fought for pensions not being paid to the Muslims? And an at one point the party and the party leaders put a ban on that and I had a host of problems to lift the blockade from paying pensions to the Muslims. Would I have been firm enough if I had organised parties across the river Drina? Other people did that. I didn't do that. Would I have been firm if I had not proposed that Muslims should be members of the government and judges? I proposed those things at the beginning in May, June, when people were put forward for the municipal bodies. I proposed Muslims and Croats everywhere. Unlike Ostojic and the likes of him, I did not want the apartments to be occupied permanently. I was in favour of temporary decisions for the occupation of apartments. One had to have enough power and force to fight for that, and many used that and they related to some other concepts. He had a different opinion. That is why there was always a hostility of the party and the party leadership towards me. And that animosity existed towards me. In other words, you have to bear that in mind. It was a very difficult when you have only one party, only one set of mind and the conditions such as they were, it was very difficult to fight for some normal things. One had to have courage. One had to have courage to resign and to leave at a certain point. Why did the others not do that? I was not power thirsty then, I'm not now. If you can do things in a normal way, if you can find normal solutions, fine. If that is not the case, well, one of those people was Ostojic. He was -- I remember that there were rumours. I would not remember those rumours if they -- if he was not in the centre of those rumours and if he had not been forced to graze grass. I mean, that is what lingers in my memory from those times. It would not linger if he wasn't the way he was, I mean, I have -- well, I don't know anything. I have just -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, we've heard evidence that Mr. Ostojic himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour the transcript reference is 26686, Judge, His Honour Judge Hanoteau asked some questions at that time for two or three pages. I'll start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, by any chance would you have the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It was the 4th of July an easy to remember date, I think. Sorry, I didn't mean that at all rudely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, Mr. Ostojic -- there was evidence that Mr. Ostojic told all the members of the cabinet, the government, about this incident when he said he had been, quite badly in his view, maltreated by the yellow wasps. Is that right, that all the members of the government, cabinet, including you, were told by Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that he told that to the cabinet members. I heard it on the grapevine from those sources. I know all that. I don't know that he told the story to the government. I can't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say, again, whether you can be clear that he didn't tell you directly or that you just don't remember whether he did?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't remember. Quite simply I don't remember. But I mean, I'm saying that I heard rumours about that. I heard it on the grapevine. I heard about that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you yourself involved in any follow-up to that incident involving the yellow wasps and Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What do you mean when you say follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, were you involved in any action in response to Mr. Ostojic's reported ill treatment at the hands of the yellow wasps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Quite simply, I don't think that would be something that I would deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know what was done about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know any details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know about any actions of Mr. Davidovic in relation to yellow wasps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour give me a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've no further questions of Mr. Djeric. But, Your Honour, I think it likely -- we have discussed the matter as we always do and should. I think it's nevertheless likely that Mr. Krajisnik may ask Your Honours for an opportunity to put questions himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, would you wish to put any additional question to Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have only two questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then before I give you an opportunity to put those questions to Mr. Djeric, Mr. Krajisnik, you're instructed not to introduce questions by referring to -- that is about misunderstandings or these kind of things with certain inappropriate context, and so therefore you should refrain from that and you should address the witness either by his family name or, as -- so Mr. Djeric or Witness. That's all fine. It should not in any way get the atmosphere of people who know each other and know what one expects from one another. That's -- you may put questions to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Momo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd also like you to address Mr. Krajisnik as everyone does in this courtroom, that's Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Krajisnik addresses you as Mr. Djeric. Yes? Please. Please, well, you exchanged a good afternoon. Mr. Krajisnik, put your question to Mr. Djeric, or your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Djeric, did Mr. Djokanovic ever tell you about some crimes that had taken place in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well, then. With this regard --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would he tell me anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember. And whether there would have been any reason to tell you is not what Mr. Krajisnik asked you. So if he would like to know, he'll certainly ask you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I'm asking this because Mr. Djokanovic testified before this Trial Chamber and your answer, "I don't know," is satisfactory. I just want to know whether you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I don't remember any such thing because Mr. Djokanovic spent most of his time down there. You know that he was in Koljevic's office, in Radovan's office. He was not in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well, then. Second question: Since you said that you know Mr. Davidovic, do you remember that Mr. Davidovic provided security in April and May, the government, on Mount Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't remember that. Mr. Krajisnik, I met Davidovic in Bijeljina, in Bijeljina, when I had a meeting there. He was there with a unit, I don't know which unit that was, and he introduced himself to me and that's how I got to know him. I don't know anything about what happened to him later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: These were the only two questions that I had. Thank you very much. I'm satisfied with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you very much. I would like to thank the witness, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need for -- the Bench has no further questions. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, this means that this concludes your evidence in this Court. I'd like to thank you for having come to The Hague and for having answered questions from the Bench, Prosecution and Defence, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher would you please escort Mr. Djeric out of the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank you deeply and -- thank you. I would like to thank you the auditorium as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In order to keep matters as neutral as possible, and also because I expressly asked the parties not to deal with certain matters in this courtroom, it's my suggestion that we strike off the record, although appreciated, the irrelevant remark from Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, that does not mean that it's not in my ears any more, it just means that it's not on paper any more. Unless any of the parties would disagree I would like to have page 44, lines 10 up to and including 17 out, stricken from the record. I see nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I should say I apologise perhaps it was remiss of me not have to have passed on your request specifically to Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not spend any more words about it. Yes. Then I -- there are a few matters -- of minor matters, I would say, which I'd like to deal with. The first one is we discussed earlier today the issue of tendering a selection from the bridge negotiations video. Is there any agreement yet reached by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What I was going to suggest, and I know my learned friends are agreeable to, is that the registrar assigns one number now to the bridge video, a second number now to the Islamic declaration, and that the parties abide by the timetable in relation to exhibits, to provide the relevant documentation, one to the Registry and two to the Chamber. In other words, no documents will be handed up at this moment but numbers will be assigned. That's our agreed suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber follows the suggestion of the parties. Mr. Registrar, you're invited to at this moment assign two exhibit numbers although we haven't received the exhibit yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
